subject: 소나타 형식의 논리
title: A musical argument in three stages
content: Sonata form organises a movement into three large sections, and its logic is closer to an argument than to a story. Material is presented in two contrasting keys, then developed and destabilised, then restated with the conflict resolved, and the whole design turns on the relationship between those keys rather than on the melodies themselves. The exposition establishes the problem. A first group of material appears in the home key, a transition modulates, and a second group appears in a related key, so the movement now contains two areas of tonal stability that do not agree. Composers marked this section for repetition, since a listener who has not registered the two keys cannot follow what comes next. The development destabilises everything. Fragments of the earlier material are combined, transposed, and passed between voices while the harmony moves restlessly, so no key holds long enough to feel like home, and the tension accumulates from that instability rather than from any thematic drama. This is the section where composers differ most, and its length varies enormously across the tradition. The recapitulation resolves by transposition. The same material returns, and the second group now appears in the home key rather than in the contrasting one, so the disagreement that opened the movement is settled by bringing everything into one tonal area. A listener who did not register the original conflict hears only a repetition. This explains why the form dominated instrumental music for a century and a half. It supplies a large structure that requires no text and no programme, since the argument is conducted in the relationship between keys, and audiences trained on the convention followed it without any of it being explained.

subject: 타악 합주의 구조
title: Ensembles where the melody is shared out
content: Several traditions build ensembles almost entirely from tuned percussion, and their music is organised on a principle that European practice does not use. A melody is distributed among many instruments so that no single player performs it, and the line emerges from the combination rather than from any individual part. The technique is interlocking. Two or more players are given complementary patterns, each containing rests where the other sounds, and the resulting composite runs faster than any of them plays. Musicians describe learning their own part without ever practising the melody it helps produce, and a player hearing their part alone would not recognise the piece. Tuning belongs to the ensemble rather than to the instrument. Sets are tuned together and cannot be exchanged between groups, since pairs of instruments are deliberately tuned slightly apart to produce a shimmer when they sound together, and the rate of that beating is a characteristic of the particular set. An instrument removed from its ensemble is unusable. Structure is cyclical rather than developmental. A piece repeats a cycle marked by a large gong at its end, with faster instruments subdividing the same span, so the form is a set of nested layers rather than a sequence of events. Signals from a drum indicate changes of tempo and of section to the whole group. Learning happens without notation in most such traditions. Players absorb their parts in ensemble from childhood, the repertoire is held collectively, and written scores were introduced only recently and mainly for teaching outsiders, which practitioners regard as a different way of knowing the same music.

subject: 풍속화가 남긴 일상
title: Paintings of people doing ordinary things
content: A genre depicting everyday activity — working, travelling, drinking, quarrelling, playing — developed in several traditions and supplies historians with evidence that formal art does not. Portraits show what people wished to appear; these paintings show what they did, or at least what a painter thought worth recording. The subjects were considered low. Hierarchies of genre placed historical and religious subjects at the top and scenes of common life near the bottom, so painters working in this category were ranked accordingly, and their work was collected by people outside the highest circles. That marginal status is why so much of it was not preserved carefully. The detail is unusually reliable. A painter recording a market, a wrestling match, or a school had no reason to idealise the tools, clothing, and postures involved, so the material culture depicted can be checked against excavated objects and generally matches. Historians use such images for exactly this. Humour is frequently present. Figures are caught mid gesture, drunk, cheating, or distracted, and the painter's attitude toward them ranges from affection to mockery, so the pictures record attitudes as well as activities. Determining which is which requires knowing the conventions of the tradition. Reception changed completely. Work dismissed in its own time as trivial has become, for later audiences, the most immediately engaging art of its period, since a scene of ordinary life needs no explanation while a religious allegory does. Museums now display such paintings prominently, which reverses the arrangement their makers knew.

subject: 두루마리와 보는 순서
title: A painting you unroll a section at a time
content: A handscroll is not viewed all at once. It is held in the hands, unrolled from right to left, and read section by section with only an arm's width visible at any moment, so the work unfolds in time and the viewer controls the pace. This makes it closer to reading than to looking at a picture. Composition follows the viewing. Painters arranged elements so that each visible span works as an image while the transitions between spans carry the movement, and a scene can therefore build, resolve, and give way to another as the hands move. Passages of empty space function as intervals between episodes, which is a use of blankness that a hanging picture cannot exploit. Narrative scrolls exploit the sequence directly. A story unfolds as the viewer advances, characters reappear in successive scenes, and time passes as the scroll passes, so the same figure may appear several times in what a photograph would present as one image. Reading such a work as a single composition misunderstands it entirely. The format governs how the work is stored and shared. A scroll is rolled, boxed, and brought out for a guest, unrolled slowly on a table while both parties look, and then put away, so viewing is an occasion involving conversation rather than a solitary encounter with something on a wall. Colophons record those occasions. Later viewers wrote comments, poems, and seals onto the end of the scroll, so the object accumulates a record of everybody who examined it, and unrolling a famous work eventually means passing through several centuries of responses before reaching the painting.

subject: 옹기의 숨 쉬는 벽
title: Pottery made deliberately porous
content: Large storage vessels in the Korean tradition are fired at a temperature that leaves the body slightly porous, and the porosity is intentional. Fermented foods stored in them require slow gas exchange, so a wall that is completely sealed would produce a different result, and the craft was developed around exactly this requirement. The glaze contributes to the effect. A coating made from wood ash and clay melts into a thin uneven layer that seals the surface against liquid while leaving microscopic passages, so the vessel holds brine without leaking and still permits air to move. Vessels glazed with a fully vitrified coating fail at the purpose. Firing temperature is the controlling variable. Too low and the body is weak and absorbs liquid; too high and it becomes impervious, and the working range is narrow enough that kiln management determined whether a batch was usable. Traditional kilns built into a slope allowed the maker to hold the temperature within that band. Size shaped the technique. The largest vessels stand taller than a person and cannot be thrown in one piece, so the maker builds them in stages from coils or slabs, allowing each section to stiffen before adding the next, and a single vessel may take days. Placement completes the system. Such vessels were kept outdoors on a raised platform, where daily temperature changes drive the exchange that the porous wall permits, so the pottery, the food, and the arrangement of the household worked together, and moving the vessels indoors alters the result.

subject: 담장의 종류와 시선
title: Walls that control what can be seen
content: A boundary wall does more than mark property. Its height, its material, and whether it can be seen through determine what passers-by know about the household, and traditions that built many kinds of wall used the differences deliberately. A solid high wall conceals completely. It states that what happens inside is not public, and it appears where privacy or security mattered most, so its use in a settlement maps onto who had something to protect. Such walls also darken the space inside them, which is a cost that builders accepted where the concealment was worth it. A low wall marks without hiding. A boundary at waist height defines a space while leaving it visible, so a household using one is asserting a claim without withdrawing, and courtyards enclosed this way remain part of the street in a way that high walls prevent. Material carries meaning. Stone, brick, packed earth, and woven fence each announce what the household could afford and what the region supplied, and decorative patterning in brick or tile appears where the wall was meant to be admired rather than merely to function. Some traditions treated the wall as a display surface. Openings control the view precisely. A gate, a window in a wall, or a section of open lattice frames a particular sight — a tree, a rock, a distant hill — so the wall becomes an instrument for composing what is seen rather than only for blocking it. Garden traditions developed this into a technique with its own vocabulary.

subject: 창호가 거르는 빛
title: Paper windows and the light they make
content: Windows covered with paper stretched over a wooden lattice produce a quality of interior light that glass does not. The paper scatters what passes through it, so the room receives illumination from the whole window surface rather than a bright patch and deep shadow, and everything inside is lit softly and evenly. The lattice is structural and visual. Thin wooden members divide the opening into a pattern that supports the paper and casts a faint grid onto the floor, and the density of that pattern varies by region and by the room's purpose, so a lattice is chosen for how much light it admits and for how it looks from both sides. Layers add control. Some windows carry paper on one side of the lattice and some on both, which traps air between and improves insulation, and doubled paper diffuses more strongly, so the choice trades light for warmth. Households adjusted this seasonally. The material behaves with the weather. Paper passes water vapour, so a room enclosed this way does not accumulate damp, and it tightens or slackens with humidity, which produces the drumlike sound that residents of such buildings describe. Rain and wind are audible through it in a way that glass prevents. Replacement was a household task. Paper yellows, tears, and loses tension, so it was renewed periodically — traditionally before a major seasonal occasion — and the practice of repapering marked the calendar. A small piece of a leaf or flower was sometimes pressed into the paper at a corner, which appears as a shadow when the window is lit from outside.

subject: 씻김굿의 절차
title: A ceremony performed to release the dead
content: A ritual in the Korean shamanic tradition is performed for somebody who has died, with the stated purpose of resolving whatever the deceased left unsettled so that they may depart. It proceeds through a fixed sequence over many hours, and the structure is as prescribed as any theatrical form. The opening prepares the space. Offerings are arranged, the site is purified, and spirits are invited, so the ordinary room becomes a place where the ceremony can occur, and this framing occupies a substantial portion of the whole. Participants describe the transition as the point at which ordinary behaviour stops. The central sequence addresses the deceased directly. The officiant speaks in the voice of the dead person, delivering what they are held to have left unsaid, and family members reply, weep, and occasionally argue, so the ceremony supplies an occasion for saying what could not be said while the person lived. Observers consistently identify this as its work. Objects carry the action. A length of cloth is drawn through a knotted state and released, a vessel of water is used for washing, and the untying is performed physically in view of everybody, so the resolution is enacted rather than described. The symbolism is direct enough that participants unfamiliar with the tradition follow it. Music sustains the whole. Percussion and singing continue through the sequence, with rhythmic patterns marking each stage, and the musicians are specialists who work with the officiant regularly. The practice has been documented extensively by folklorists and is now performed both as ritual and as staged performance, which practitioners distinguish sharply.

subject: 가면 무용의 지역차
title: The same masked drama in different valleys
content: Masked dance dramas performed in different regions of one country share a broad structure while differing in ways that a specialist reads immediately. The differences record how each community adapted an inherited form, and comparing them shows what a tradition preserves and what it lets go. The stock characters recur everywhere. A corrupt official, a lecherous monk, a wronged wife, and a servant who mocks his superiors appear across regions, so the satirical targets were shared, and the durability of these figures across communities that had little contact indicates how widely the grievances were felt. Masks differ sharply. Materials range from paper and gourd to carved wood, colours and exaggerations vary, and some regions burn their masks after each performance while others treat them as heirlooms. Where masks are destroyed, no historical examples survive, so the documentary record is uneven for reasons internal to the traditions. Music and dance vocabulary vary with local practice. The percussion patterns are those of the region's other music, the dance draws on movements the community already knew, and a performer trained in one region cannot simply perform another's version. This is what makes them distinct traditions rather than variants. Text is the least stable element. The plays were transmitted orally, performers improvised, and the versions recorded by collectors in the twentieth century differ substantially in dialogue while agreeing on the sequence of episodes, which is the pattern that oral transmission generally produces. Designation as heritage has frozen particular versions. Each regional form now has an authorised text and a designated holder, which preserves it and ends the variation that produced the differences in the first place.

subject: 설화가 전해지는 방식
title: Stories that nobody wrote and everybody knows
content: Folk narratives circulate without an author, change as they pass, and yet remain recognisable across enormous distances. Understanding how they hold their shape while altering their details reveals something about how oral transmission actually works. The plot survives; the surface does not. Comparative study has shown that the same sequence of events appears in versions collected thousands of kilometres apart, with different names, settings, animals, and objects, so what transmits is a structure rather than a text. Indexes classifying tale types were built on exactly this observation. Local detail is supplied by the teller. A story arriving in a new region acquires that region's landscape, occupations, foods, and social arrangements, since a teller narrates from what their audience knows, and the resulting version feels indigenous. This is why the same tale can be claimed as national property by several countries. Function shapes the ending. The same story may conclude with a reward, a punishment, or a joke depending on who is telling it and why, and versions collected from children differ systematically from those collected from adults. Collectors who recorded only one audience produced a distorted picture. Repetition aids memory. Threefold structures, formulaic openings, and repeated dialogue appear across unrelated traditions because they make a story easier to hold and to reproduce, so the features that strike literary readers as primitive are the mechanism of survival. Writing changes the transmission. Once a version is printed, it acquires an authority the oral versions never had, and later tellers converge on it, so the act of collecting a living tradition tends to end the variation that made it living.

subject: 기행문의 시선
title: Writing about a place you are passing through
content: Travel writing is produced by somebody who does not live where they are writing about, and everything characteristic of the form follows from that position. The writer notices what residents no longer see and misunderstands what residents take for granted, and both are structural rather than personal failings. Selection reveals the writer. What strikes a traveller as worth recording is determined by what is unfamiliar, so a travel account is simultaneously a description of a place and an inventory of the writer's assumptions, and later readers frequently learn more about the writer's own society from the comparisons drawn. Historians use such texts in exactly this double way. The genre carries a long problem with authority. A traveller claims to report what they saw, readers cannot check, and the tradition contains a great deal of invention presented as observation, including accounts of places the author never reached. Establishing what a given text actually witnessed is a standard scholarly task. Encounter is the recurring difficulty. Describing people met on the road requires deciding whether they are individuals or examples, and the tradition slides constantly between the two, so the same passage may record a specific conversation and generalise it into a claim about a population. Readers rarely notice the transition. The best examples acknowledge the position. A writer who states what they could not understand, records their own errors, and distinguishes what they saw from what they were told produces something more useful than one who reports confidently, and the tradition's most durable works are conspicuously those that admit the limits of a passing view.

subject: 음반 재킷의 시각화
title: Making a picture for something you hear
content: A record sleeve must stand for music in a picture, which is a problem with no right answer. A picture cannot show sound, so it works by what it calls to mind, by showing the player, or by setting a mood, and the rules that grew up differ sharply between kinds of music. The format itself shaped the art. A large square viewed at arm's length gave designers a substantial surface, and the period when records were that size produced work that is collected and exhibited independently of the music. Smaller formats and then screens reduced the surface, and designs migrated toward images that survive reduction to a thumbnail. Portraiture dominates in some traditions. Where the performer's identity is central, the sleeve shows them, and the pose, setting, and treatment position the music before anybody hears it. Traditions where the composition rather than the performer is the subject developed abstract and typographic approaches instead. A house look competes with a design for one release. Some labels imposed a consistent format across every release, so a buyer recognised the label before the title, and those catalogues are now studied as design programmes. Others gave each release its own treatment, which produces variety and loses the shelf recognition. The sleeve also carried information. Notes on the back supplied context, credits, and frequently an essay, and for many listeners that text was the only writing about the music they encountered, so the format functioned as a publishing platform. Its disappearance removed a channel that nothing has quite replaced. The back of the sleeve did work too. Notes, credits, and a short essay gave a buyer something to read while the record played, and for many people that text was the only writing about the music they ever saw. When the format shrank, that reading went with it.

subject: 본문 서체 고르기
title: Choosing the type a book is set in
content: A book's text face is chosen before a word is typeset, and the choice affects how long the reading feels, how many pages the book runs to, and what impression the writing makes. Readers almost never notice the face and are affected by it throughout. Legibility at small size is the first requirement. A face designed for headlines has fine strokes and tight spacing that disappear at ten points, while a text face has sturdier stems, open counters, and generous spacing between letters, so the categories are not interchangeable however similar they look enlarged. Set width determines extent. Faces differ in how much horizontal space the same words occupy, and a book set in a wide face runs to more pages, costs more to print, and feels longer to read, so publishers with a fixed page budget choose accordingly. This is a commercial decision presented as a design one. Historical association arrives with the shapes. A face modelled on Renaissance printing carries one set of associations, one designed in the twentieth century carries another, and a reader who could not name either responds to the difference, which is why period fiction and technical manuals are set differently. Colour on the page is the deciding factor for many designers. The overall grey of a block of text depends on stroke weight, spacing, and the space between lines, and a face that produces an even texture is restful while one that produces uneven patches tires the eye. Designers judge this by printing a page and looking at it from a distance, blurred, which removes the words and leaves the texture.

subject: 명절 음식의 상징
title: Food that is eaten only once a year
content: Dishes made for a festival are often slow, costly, and cooked at no other time of year, and their survival is not explained by taste. What such food accomplishes is marking the occasion, and the difficulty of making it is part of how the marking works. Effort signals the occasion. A dish that takes a whole day says that the day is not ordinary, and homes that no longer make it say the festival feels thinner, which suggests the work rather than the food carries the meaning. Convenience versions exist and are described by participants as not quite the thing. Shape and ingredient carry meaning explicitly in many traditions. Round shapes for wholeness, long noodles for long life, stacked layers for gain, and grains tied to the season turn up in cultures with no link, and people can usually say what each one means when asked. The explanations are sometimes late inventions and the practice is old. Distribution matters as much as consumption. Such food is shared with neighbours, offered to ancestors, or given to those who have less, so the preparation supports an exchange that the ordinary calendar does not require. Households that stopped the preparation frequently stopped the exchange with it. The dishes preserve older foodways. Because festival cooking follows old method rather than what is handy now, it keeps foods and ways that daily cooking dropped, so food historians read it as a record of what was ordinary a few lifetimes back. A festival table is therefore a document as well as a meal. Who cooks is rarely a free choice. The work falls on one part of the household by long habit, it takes days, and the burden is heavy enough that some families now buy what they once made. Those who still cook say the day feels different when they do.

subject: 저장 기술과 계절
title: Making food last until the next harvest
content: Before refrigeration, a settled population had to move its autumn abundance into winter and spring, and the techniques developed for this shaped cuisines more decisively than any preference. What a culture eats in February is determined by what it could preserve in October. Drying is the most widespread method. Removing water stops decay, and traditions dried fish, meat, fruit, grain, and vegetables wherever the climate permitted, so the dried form became a distinct ingredient with its own uses rather than a substitute for the fresh one. Many cuisines now use both and treat them as different foods. Salting and fermentation work by controlling what grows. Salt suppresses spoilage organisms while permitting others, and the resulting transformation produces flavours that could not be obtained otherwise, so a method adopted for necessity became a source of what a cuisine tastes like. Traditions with a long cold season developed the most elaborate versions. Cold storage exploited what the landscape offered. Pits, caves, ice houses, and buried vessels held root vegetables and fermented goods at stable temperatures, and buildings were designed around them, so architecture records the preservation calendar. Households organised space by season accordingly. The work was concentrated and communal. Preparing a winter's supply required more hands than one household had, so neighbours worked in rotation, and the resulting gatherings became social occasions with their own customs. Where refrigeration removed the necessity, those gatherings ended, and communities that maintain the practice now frequently describe the assembly rather than the food as what they are preserving.

subject: 다과와 손님
title: What is offered to somebody who visits
content: Nearly every culture prescribes something to set before a guest, and the prescription is remarkably specific about what, when, and how. The substance matters less than the offering, which is why refusing can be difficult and why the forms are followed even by households with little to spare. Immediacy is the common feature. Something is produced quickly, before any conversation about purpose, so the guest is received before being asked why they came, and traditions that delay this are experienced by visitors as cold. What appears may be minimal — water, tea, a single sweet — and its arrival does the work. The offering marks a threshold. Accepting it establishes that the visit has begun and that the visitor is present as a guest rather than as a passer-by, so declining is understood as declining the relationship rather than the food. Traditions accordingly develop ways of accepting minimally for those who cannot eat. Sequence encodes duration. A short visit receives one thing, a longer one receives a series, and the arrival of a further course signals that the host expects the visitor to stay, which both parties read without discussion. Guests judge when to leave partly by this. The preparation is frequently invisible and considerable. Households keep something suitable ready at all times, which requires planning that the guest never sees, and the appearance of effortlessness is itself part of the offering. In traditions where this is elaborate, the pressure falls on whoever manages the household, which is a cost that accounts of hospitality rarely mention.

subject: 통과 의례의 음식
title: Dishes that appear only at a life event
content: Birth, coming of age, marriage, and death each carry prescribed foods in most traditions, and the dishes differ from festival food in an important respect: they mark a change in a person rather than a point in the calendar. The same household may prepare them once or twice in a generation. Quantity signals the event. Such occasions require feeding everybody who attends, which for a marriage or a funeral may be the whole settlement, so the preparation is on a scale that ordinary cooking never reaches, and the resources involved announce what the household could muster. Communities assisted, and the records of who contributed were remembered. Particular items are prescribed rather than chosen. A specific grain, a specific soup, or a specific arrangement is required, and substituting is noticed, so the menu is less a matter of hospitality than of correctness. Participants can frequently state the reason, and the stated reasons vary while the practice is stable. Distribution is part of the rite. Food is offered to ancestors, shared with guests, sent to households that could not attend, and in several traditions given to those outside the community, so the preparation supports a series of transfers that mark who stands where in relation to the family. Funeral food is the most conserved. Traditions that have abandoned almost every other ceremonial requirement frequently retain what is served after a death, since the occasion admits the least improvisation, and caterers now supply it in forms that follow the old prescriptions closely.

subject: 시장 소리의 문화
title: The sound of a place where things are sold
content: A traditional market is an environment of sound as much as of sight. Calls announcing the goods, bargaining conducted aloud, the noise of preparation, and the movement of crowds combine into something that regular buyers read as easily as a shop sign. The calls are a form. A seller works up a phrase, a tune, and a beat that carry over the din and name them without a word being caught, so a buyer far off knows what is for sale and who is selling it. Such calls were inherited, taught, and in several traditions regarded as belonging to particular families. Bargaining is public by design. Bargaining aloud lets others hear what price was reached, which restrains both parties, and markets that moved to fixed prices lost that information along with the noise. Participants describe the exchange as performance with an audience. Sound maps the space. Different trades cluster, each producing its own noise — metalworking, food preparation, livestock — so a visitor navigates partly by ear, and the layout of a market is legible acoustically before it is legible visually. Recordings made by researchers have been used to reconstruct arrangements that no plan recorded. The soundscape has largely gone. Supermarkets are quiet by design, fixed prices removed bargaining, and amplified recordings replaced live calls in the markets that remain, so what survives is documented rather than heard. Several archives now hold recordings made specifically because the collectors recognised the loss as it was happening. Sellers recognised each other by ear. A trader could tell from across the rows who had come that day and what they had brought, and a new voice was noticed at once. That is a kind of knowing that a quiet shop floor does not allow.

subject: 지붕 재료와 마을 경관
title: What a village looks like depends on its roofs
content: The appearance of a traditional settlement is determined more by roofing than by anything else, since roofs occupy most of what a viewer sees from any distance. What was used depended on what grew or could be quarried nearby, so the look of a region is a map of its materials. Thatch dominates where suitable grasses or reeds grow. It insulates well, weighs little, and requires a steep pitch so that water runs off before soaking in, which is why thatched buildings have the profile they do. It also needs replacing every few decades, so the craft persisted as long as the roofs did and disappeared quickly once it stopped. Tile requires clay and fuel. Firing tiles demands kilns and organisation, so tiled roofs appear where those existed and mark the buildings of those who could afford them, which makes the ratio of tile to thatch in a settlement a record of its wealth distribution. Tiles permit a shallower pitch and last far longer. Stone slates, wooden shingles, and bark were used where those materials were abundant, each producing a distinct texture and colour, and regions are recognisable from a distance by the resulting surface. Photographs from before industrial materials show this variation clearly. Industrial roofing erased most of it. Corrugated metal and concrete tile can be transported anywhere, cost less, and last longer, so settlements across whole countries converged in appearance within a generation. Where traditional roofs are now maintained, it is usually by designation and subsidy rather than by preference, since almost nobody would choose the labour otherwise.

subject: 빨래터의 사회
title: The place where washing was done together
content: Before piped water, washing was done where water ran, and the spot became a kind of institution. Women came there often, worked side by side for hours, and what passed between them did work that no other regular meeting in their lives did. The work required the location. Rinsing needs running water in quantity, beating cloth needs a flat stone, and drying needs sun and room, so the ground chose the spot and everybody used the same one. Attendance was therefore not a choice, which is what made the gathering reliable. Information circulated there. News, plans, talks about marriages, and judgements about conduct all passed through this meeting, and those who studied such villages named it a main channel, above all for women whose movement was otherwise held in. What was said there reached the whole settlement. Songs belonged to the work. Rhythmic beating suits singing, and traditions of laundry songs were collected in several countries, with texts that are frequently frank about husbands, in-laws, and hardship — material that would not have been sung elsewhere. The privacy of an all-female gathering permitted it. Its disappearance was welcomed and it removed something. Piped water at home ended crushing labour, and nobody who did that work wishes it back, and the same change removed the one regular occasion on which a whole category of the population met without supervision. Communities that have documented the transition describe both consequences, and the sites themselves survive in several places as preserved structures that record a practice rather than serving one. The work itself was hard and cold. Cloth was soaked, beaten with a stick, wrung by hand, and carried home wet, and women did it in every season including deep winter. Nobody who did it looks back on the labour with any warmth at all.

subject: 민속 인형의 재료
title: Dolls made from what was at hand
content: Figures made for children in most traditions were constructed from materials that cost nothing — straw, cloth scraps, husk, wood offcuts, clay — and that limitation shaped their appearance far more than any idea about how a doll should look. Available material therefore determined the method. Straw is bound and tied, so figures made from it have a wrapped construction, with limbs formed by folding a bundle back on itself. Cloth is stuffed and stitched. Wood is carved or turned. Each material yields a family of forms that recurs wherever that material was used. Faces were frequently absent, although the reasons given vary. Many traditions left them blank, and the reasons given vary — religious objection to representation, the belief that a child supplies the expression, or simply that painting a face requires materials nobody had. Because no expression is fixed, the resulting figures are notably open to whatever a child projects onto them. The making was domestic and quick, and therefore left almost no trace. Such figures were produced by parents or older children in a few minutes from what was to hand, replaced when they wore out, and not preserved, so almost nothing survives from before the modern period and what is known comes from later examples and from descriptions. Commercial dolls displaced them entirely and then borrowed from them. Manufactured toys arrived with painted faces and fixed clothing, and the older forms left ordinary use within a generation, after which craft revivals reproduced them as objects for adults to purchase — the usual end of a domestic craft once its practical reason has gone. Children also made their own, and although a few were kept, most were lost. A doll built by a child from grass or rag is a different object from one made by a parent, and the few that were kept show how young hands work. Most were lost, so what we have came from adults.

subject: 팽이와 놀이의 물리
title: A toy that teaches something without saying so
content: A spinning top stays up while it turns and falls when it slows, and a child playing with one meets a law of motion long before anybody names it. Old play is full of such things, and the fact that they turn up in cultures with no link suggests the physics rather than any borrowing explains it. The behaviour is genuinely counterintuitive. A thing that would fall at once if set down still keeps its balance while spinning, and a push from the side sends it a way nobody expects, so a child handling one is finding something that defies ordinary sense. Adults frequently cannot explain it either. Construction affects performance measurably. Weight distributed toward the rim spins longer than the same mass near the axis, a lower centre of gravity is more stable, and the point's shape and material determine friction, so children who make their own tops experiment with these variables and develop reliable intuitions about them. Competitions reward exactly that knowledge. Regional forms differ in how they are launched. Whipping, string winding, hand twisting, and throwing each produce different spin rates and require different skills, and traditions are identified by the launch method as much as by the object. The associated games — knocking others out of a ring, spinning longest, striking a target — vary correspondingly. Similar principles underlie other traditional toys. Hoops, yo-yos, kites, and buzzers all work through mechanics that a player learns by handling rather than by explanation, and educators have repeatedly proposed using them for exactly that reason, with results that suggest the informal version teaches more reliably than the formalised one. Adults play with them too. Spinning contests draw crowds in several countries, the tops used are made to fine limits, and players talk about weight and point in the way that any craft talks about its tools. The toy sits at the root of a sport.

subject: 전통 색 이름 체계
title: A colour vocabulary organised by direction
content: Several East Asian traditions name five main colours and tie each to a direction, a season, an element, and a place in a larger scheme. The colours are not chosen for how they look side by side; they are chosen because the scheme calls for five, and the look follows from the system. Blue-green, red, yellow, white, and black form the set. Each carries meanings that reach well past how it looks, so using a colour is taken as calling up a direction and a season, and pairs are read as claims about relation rather than as visual choices. A viewer within the tradition sees a claim where an outsider sees a palette. The scheme governs where colours appear. Architectural decoration, ceremonial dress, and the arrangement of objects follow the directional associations, so what looks like ornament is frequently a placement rule, and a building's painted surfaces record the scheme's geometry. Intermediate colours were named as combinations. A vocabulary of secondary shades derives from pairing the principal five, which produces names describing a relationship rather than a hue, so translating them requires explaining a system rather than matching a swatch. Colour dictionaries in these traditions read quite differently from Western ones. The scheme survives where the beliefs behind it have faded. Contemporary designers use the palette knowing it as traditional rather than as cosmological, ceremonial dress retains the placements, and the associations persist in language, so a system that was once an account of how the world is organised now functions as an inherited aesthetic vocabulary. The five names came before the dyes did. Some of the colours were hard to make and stayed rare, so what the scheme called for and what a weaver could buy were not the same, and the gap shows in what survives. Cheap cloth used what was to hand.

subject: 문양의 반복과 변주
title: Why a pattern must repeat and must not be identical
content: Ornament covering a surface works by repetition, and a pattern repeating exactly produces a different effect from one that shifts slightly. Traditions differ sharply in which they pursue, and therefore that choice reveals what the ornament is for. Mechanical regularity suggests order. A pattern printed or stamped the same way across a surface reads as a system, and traditions stating rank, permanence, or divine order have used just this, with the evenness itself carrying the meaning. Any visible irregularity would undermine the statement. Handwork produces variation whether or not it is wanted. A pattern painted, carved, or woven by hand differs slightly at each repetition, and although the differences are small, they give the surface a liveliness that machine work lacks, which is why mechanical copies are so often called dead. Some traditions built variation in deliberately. Introducing a deliberate error is a recorded practice in several traditions, explained variously as humility before perfection, as a way of preventing a pattern from trapping a spirit, or as a maker's signature. Whether the explanations are original or supplied later, the errors exist and are locatable. The structure beneath is mathematical. A repeating pattern falls into one of a small number of symmetry types, set by geometry rather than by culture, and surveys of ornament from many traditions find that most of those types turn up in most large traditions. What differs is which are favoured, which is a matter of taste operating within a set of options that nobody chose. A weaver therefore cannot avoid the choice. Every row of a woven band either repeats what came before or does not, and the decision is made hundreds of times in an hour, so a pattern records a great many small choices that nobody planned as a whole.
